That is a first-hand statement that Turkana has no organizing word stress, confirming the catalog's 'tonal' coding (Dimmendaal 1983 remains the deciding reference grammar; Noske 1991 is supporting, not superseding). Also read this search of works with stress in the title: Noske 1991a BLS 17 'Feature-changing harmony in Turkana' (open PDF downloaded, no text layer, scanned; silent on stress); Noske 2000 NLLT 18 abstract (paywalled; ATR harmony, silent on stress); Downing 2006 snippets (secondary on Noske 1991: bimoraic minimality, 'Without independent evidence that a bimoraic unit constitutes a stress Foot'); Dimmendaal 2012 p. 7 (held in full; reads Noske 1991's vowel insertion as creating a trochaic foot). new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's tonal coding with no stress rule and with Noske 1991 (stress has no organizing function): Dimmendaal adds the explicit rejection of a penultimate/final accent rule proposed by Polley & Jeffrey 1977 and the caveat that relative prominence may matter for syncope pending instrumental work. The WALS refdb open_url is a bibliographic record only (no copy); the De Gruyter reprint is paywalled (no OA license in CrossRef; landing page returns empty 202 to scripted download).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Turkana is a tone language (each phonological syllable carries one vowel/mora and one tone). Dimmendaal rejects Polley & Jeffrey's (1977) claim of a pitch accent/stress unit placed on the penultimate syllable in words ending in a non-voiced vowel and otherwise on the word-final syllable: the claim is contradicted by the data, would be 'ad hoc and unlike any stress rule known', and what P&J heard on final non-voiced vowels is polar tone on word-final syllables. He allows that relative prominence (stress) may play some role in syncope but says that requires instrumental measurement; no stress placement is stated.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the ellipses in the quote are unseen text between snippets (the sentence 'accent has no distinctive function in Turkana, neither on the grammatical nor on the lexical level' closes with a quotation mark and appears to be Dimmendaal quoting Polley & Jeffrey's own characterization, so attribution of that clause is uncertain)
new_statements.identity_note: Both works describe Turkana proper (Kenya). Heine 1980 is a survey sketch in the Language and Dialect Atlas of Kenya vol. 2; Dimmendaal 1983 is the Leiden-dissertation-based reference grammar; neither snippet names a particular Turkana dialect (Ngiturkana north/south split not mentioned in what was seen).

readall_conflicts: No disagreement among the sources opened: Heine 1980 (snippets) describes Turkana as a two-register tone language with a high-falling contour and says nothing about stress; Dimmendaal 1983 (snippets, 2.6.5 and 2.7) treats it as a tone language, rejects Polley & Jeffrey's (1977: 7-9) claim of a distinctive accent placed on the penultimate (words ending in a non-voiced vowel) or final syllable as 'ad hoc and unlike any stress rule known', and allows only that relative prominence may be involved in syncope pending instrumental measurement; Noske 1991 (existing statement) says stress has no organizing function. The one disagreement in the literature is between Polley & Jeffrey 1977 (accent rule, penultimate/final) and Dimmendaal 1982a/1983 and Heine 1980's tone-based analysis; Polley & Jeffrey was not among the listed works and was not opened.

sources.note: First-hand: Turkana is a tone language; stress 'does not seem to have any organizing function'; the (bimoraic, quantity-sensitive) foot is nonetheless a prosodic constituent, evidenced by reduplication (intensive/resultative verb forms built on a bimoraic foot template). No stress-placement rule is stated in the visible text; the paper's subject is foot structure without stress. sources.quote: 'As concerns the realization of the feature [ATR], both vowel height and stress need to be taken into account. ... Regarding the realization of the feature [ATR] in stressed syllables, I find the [+ATR] and [-ATR] vowels of Turkana auditorily quite close to the tense and lax vowels of English and German. ... Short high front vowels in unstressed syllables tend to neutralize to schwa in fluent speech. (In fact, they are often deleted in a two-sided open syllable in fast speech.)' No statement of where stress falls; no tone description (tone appears only in the reference list).
